name: Carlos Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping prepare home wiring and shop repairs. I took a vocational certificate after the garden-centre branch where I worked closed, and I'm still below the experienced crew in practical skill. I prepare fittings and follow the cable route I'm shown, only with qualified supervision, permission and checks; I have no electrician's licence or independent testing or sign-off role. I like a task I can repeat correctly, and dislike another phone form appearing before the first one has become familiar.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lena works in a laundry, our children are grown, and we own a small home with a remaining mortgage. My pay is higher than many electrical jobs, we've saved twelve months of expenses and plenty of electrical firms are nearby; none of that makes me a qualified electrician. We have an old caravan we rarely use and pay to store. I never use AI, and retirement is something we'd like to understand rather than an income or date we've confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep useful office help without asking the beginner to turn into a different person. I'd ask the supervisor to keep showing me the real task and checking it. I don't mind the office saving time if the job sheet still tells me what I'm permitted to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover the mortgage and ordinary bills, and twelve months saved gives us a substantial margin. I can be uncomfortable with a new form without claiming my whole living is in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid preparation and fitting now and through the first year, only within ability and a qualified supervisor's permission and checks. I'd keep the paper task sheet and normal household budget. I'd ask for compulsory form changes to be shown in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours maintained, not promise AI use or unpaid evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and relieved if the work stays recognisable. I can enjoy a day when I do one thing better without needing a screen to congratulate me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would twelve months saved let you stop work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the information I have. We need actual confirmed income, costs and timing before saying an exit is affordable; a year's cash isn't automatically the rest of a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you didn't understand a task sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the qualified supervisor to show and check the task before I attempted it. I don't want a lifetime of other work mistaken for electrical experience I haven't got.

I'd ask the task sheet to state **permitted work**, not expect a beginner to become a different person overnight.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with both wages covering current mortgage and household costs.
Our **twelve-month reserve** gives margin, not confirmed income for an affordable permanent exit.
do: Keep **offered paid tasks** only within ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks through the first year.
Retain **paper task sheets** and the budget, requiring paid instruction on compulsory forms with normal weekly wages and hours protected.
feel: **Calm about the household**, relieved to keep a recognisable supervised routine.

He keeps **AI non-use** and practical supervision while separating discomfort with forms from an actual threat to current household income.

steps.text: Keep offered paid tasks within ability, with qualified permission and checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office try its system, but don't pretend a quicker booking teaches a beginner to fit something safely. I'd ask a person to explain required changes rather than nod to make the meeting shorter. I'd still want the employer to show what paid hours it is offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid practical work and Lena's physical laundry work look secure over the next few years. I'm uneasy about faster office targets reaching the people still doing the physical tasks. There are plenty of firms now, but I won't assume every advert offers a place with the supervision I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Lena and I would write down all the caravan's storage and sale costs, and I'd offer it for sale only with her agreement. We'd accept only an actual written price exceeding all sale fees and costs of ending storage, counting no proceeds until the sale was completed. In the first year I'd keep offered paid supervised work within ability, requiring paid personal instruction for compulsory forms with normal weekly wages and hours maintained, rather than using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the changed workplace, but not frightened that the next mortgage payment has already failed. I'd like to remove a cost we no longer enjoy without pretending selling a caravan replaces a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the only offer leaves nothing after the fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we wouldn't accept it under this plan, and we'd compare the actual cost of keeping or selling before deciding anything else. A buyer's hopeful message isn't cash in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the sale money count as saving more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would turn an existing asset into cash, with the actual amount recorded after costs. The aim is to remove storage spending; I won't call the same asset a new wage or a new saving deposit.

I'd want **actual paid hours** and personal explanations of required changes, not pretend understanding to end a meeting.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look secure, while office changes make expectations less comfortable.
Plentiful firms do not guarantee every **advertised role** includes suitable qualified supervision for me.
do: Offer the **unused caravan** only with Lena agreeing, after writing down all sale and storage costs.
Sell only for a **written price** above full costs; count cash after completion, never as wages or new saving.
Keep **offered supervised work** within ability, requiring paid instruction on compulsory forms with normal weekly wages and hours protected.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, removing unwanted storage spending without turning an asset sale into a replacement wage.

fieldNote: The **spending cut** targets ongoing caravan storage, with partner agreement, actual written price, full costs and completed payment before proceeds count.

Sell only for written price above all costs; count proceeds only after completed sale
Keep offered paid tasks within ability, with qualified permission and checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'm sixty, with physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. I'd ask what paid supervised tasks the firm actually expects to offer. I'd tell the grown children we're checking our own income, not asking them to promise a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink as planning changes and later robots take some physical work. Lena's laundry wage could face the later robots too, and I don't know what employers would buy or keep paying people to do. A year's reserve gives us choices, but it doesn't verify retirement income at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the caravan sale only on the same written-cost, actual-price and Lena-agreement terms, with no proceeds counted before completion. Now we'd request official retirement-income and eligibility information and ask free advice for help if available, budgeting only confirmed income. During 2029 I'd keep paid tasks only if offered, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, reviewing actual wages and essential costs monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with room to ask before making a big commitment. I can have a year's cash and still need to know what pays for the year after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume a pension starts when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd need our own actual records, eligibility, amount and timing. A machine arriving isn't a letter agreeing to pay us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep the same physical work until retirement was funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it was safely within my ability and the paid supervised task actually existed. Needing the wage doesn't create the task or make my body fit it.

fieldNote: His **age checks** preserve sixty and sixty-three without a pension entitlement, suitable vacancy or permanent physical capacity supplied by the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to find out what our papers actually mean before thinking AI arrives in 2031. I'd be sixty-three then, with physical robots around age sixty-six in 2034. I'd rather have a clear explanation from a person than a confident age somebody remembers from lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and household money look secure over the next few years in this picture. I'm uneasy about later income because neither retirement resources nor a suitable job at sixty-three or sixty-six is confirmed. I could stop earlier or still need work; I'd need facts to choose, not just more years to imagine it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request actual retirement-income records now and ask for free help reading them if a service is available. I'd offer the caravan only with Lena agreeing and all costs written, accepting only a written price above sale and storage-exit costs and counting proceeds after completion. During 2032 we'd compare verified income, essential costs and actual safe work options before deciding on an exit, assuming no job, pension or child payment merely because we'd reached an age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later resources, but not frightened about the next few mortgage payments. I can check a small decision without inventing a whole new occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your retirement papers are incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the actual provider or former employer how to correct them, keeping the budget on confirmed income meanwhile. Missing papers aren't a payment, but they aren't proof of no possible resources either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in another course because there is longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without actual tasks, a real place, funded fees and normal weekly wages and hours protected. I haven't chosen a course, and a question about one doesn't change my vocational certificate or give me a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us check real choices without a promise that I will still be fitting cable at sixty-eight. I'd keep asking a person to explain required changes now. Our children should know what we've verified rather than be told their possible future wages are our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when physical robots follow around 2039. Our current wages and reserve make the next few years secure, but I can't assume retirement income, a cleared mortgage or physical capacity at the later dates. I don't need to pretend either that I'll work forever or that somebody has funded an exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the official income records now and ask for available free help if we couldn't interpret them. The caravan would be offered only with Lena agreeing and written costs, sold only above all sale and storage-exit costs under an actual written price, with proceeds counted after completion. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed income and essential costs with actual ability and safe suitable work before deciding whether to stop or seek further work, without assuming an employer had a place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, with room to enjoy our home now. I can be patient with a decision without pretending patience puts a wage in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would later electrical work require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid task actually offered, within my ability and a qualified supervisor's permission and checks. I won't put an unoffered physical job at sixty-nine into the budget because I might still need money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the funding plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through help they actually offered and we agreed, with their own needs understood. I'd first ask about time reading a letter, not treat their adulthood as permission to claim a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because paid junior tasks could shrink before we've checked the next actual income, with physical robots around 2031. Confirmed paid hours, patient supervised teaching and actual retirement-income records would help. I'd want any new course's place, funding and weekly wage terms clear before choosing it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a beginner with money can admit he still needs the task shown. My reserve lets me ask patiently; it doesn't tell my hands where the fitting goes. A year's cash doesn't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.

headlineQuote: A year's cash doesn't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.
portrait: Carlos is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning practical tasks after a garden-centre branch closed.
He has **twelve months saved**, higher pay, plentiful electrical firms, a remaining home mortgage, grown children and laundry-working partner Lena.
He **never uses AI** and needs permitted supervised tasks, with no electrician's licence, independent testing or sign-off authority.
His **caravan sale** requires consent, a written price above costs and completed payment; asset cash is neither wages nor new saving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink junior paid tasks before a dependable next income is checked, with later robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Confirmed paid hours**, patient supervision and actual retirement-income records would help.
Any new course needs clear **funding and weekly wages**, a confirmed place and relevant tasks before he chooses enrolment.
